literal: From the grandfather Verus: the good-charactered and unangered.
prose: From my grandfather Verus I learned good character and freedom from anger.

literal: From the reputation and memory of the one who begot [me]: the modest and the manly.
prose: From the reputation and memory of my father, I learned modesty and manliness.

literal: From the mother: the piety and generosity and refraining—not only from the doing-wrong, but also from the coming-to-be of such a thought; still further: the simple according to the manner-of-living, and far from the rich manner-of-living.
prose: From my mother: piety and generosity, and refraining not only from doing wrong but even from entertaining the thought of doing so; she also taught me simplicity in one's way of living, far removed from the manner of the rich.

literal: From the great-grandfather: the not into public schools to have attended, and the to have used good teachers according to house: and the to have known, that into such things it is necessary unstintingly to be spending.
prose: From my great-grandfather: not to have attended public schools, but to have had good teachers at home, and to recognize that on such things one ought to be spending unstintingly.

literal: From the tutor: the not either Prasian, or Venetian, or Palmularius or Scutarius to become: and the toil-enduring and content-with-little: and the self-working and unmeddlesome: and the being-slow-to-accept of slander:
prose: From my tutor, I learned not to become a devoted partisan of the Greens or the Blues at the races, nor a supporter of the Parmularius or Scutarius gladiators in the arena; also to endure toil and to need little; to work with my own hands and not meddle in others' affairs; and to be slow to accept slander.

literal: From Diognetus: the not-wasting-zeal-on-vain-things: and also the being-skeptical toward the things told by miracle-workers and charlatans concerning incantations and concerning the exorcism of spirits and of the things thus spoken of: and the not to keep-quails: nor about such things to have been excited: and the enduring of frankness-of-speech: and the to-become-devoted to-philosophy: and the to-hear first indeed of-Baccheius, then also of-Tandasis and of-Marcianus: and also the to-write dialogues in childhood: and the not to desire the camp-bed-frame and the pallet-skin, and as many such things as belong to the Greek training.
prose: From Diognetus: not to waste my enthusiasm on trifles; to be skeptical toward the claims of miracle-workers and charlatans about incantations, the exorcism of spirits, and other things of that sort; not to keep quails for fighting, nor to be excitedly absorbed in such pursuits; to tolerate frankness of speech; to become devoted to philosophy, and to hear first the lectures of Baccheius, then those of Tandasis and Marcianus; also to write dialogues in my youth; and not to long for a camp-bed and a pallet-skin, and whatever else belongs to the Greek discipline of education.

literal: From Rustikos: the to-take an-impression of-the needing of-correction and of-treatment of-the character: and the not to-be-turned-aside into zeal sophistic, nor the to-write-treatises concerning theorems, nor exhortatory little-discourses to-discourse, nor phantasy-struck-ly the ascetic-man or the practical-man to-display-oneself:
prose: From Rusticus: to grasp the impression that my character needed correction and treatment; and not to turn aside into a sophist's zeal for rivalry, nor to write treatises on abstract doctrines, nor to deliver little exhortatory speeches, nor to make a showy display of oneself as an ascetic or a man of action, in a manner obsessed with impressing others.

literal: And the to-abstain-from: of rhetoric and of poetry and of elegant-wordplay. And the: not in formal-attire according-to house to-walk-about, and-not such-things to-do. And also the letters simply to-write: such as that written by him himself to my mother from Sinuessa.
prose: To abstain from rhetoric, poetry, and elegant wordplay. Also not to walk about at home dressed in formal attire, nor to do things of that sort. And to write letters in a simple, unaffected style, like the one he himself wrote to my mother from Sinuessa.

literal: And the [disposition] toward those having-grown-angry and having-erred: to be disposed easily-recalled and easily-reconciled, whenever most-quickly they themselves should-wish to-return: and the reading accurately: and the not being-satisfied while-considering-around wholly, nor to-those talking-around quickly to-assent-together: and the to-encounter [to] the Epictetean notes, of-which from-his-own-house he-shared [with me].
prose: To be easily appeased and quickly reconciled toward those who had grown angry with me or wronged me, as soon as they themselves wished to return to friendly terms; to read carefully and not be satisfied with a superficial, general grasp of a subject, nor to give quick assent to those who talk glibly around a matter; and to encounter the notes on Epictetus, copies of which he shared with me from his own household.

literal: From Apollonius: the free, and unwaveringly unrisked-to-chance, and to look to nothing else, not even for a little, or with a view to reason: and the [being] always alike, in pains sharp ones, in loss of a child, in long illnesses: and to see plainly, on the basis of a living example, that the very same [man] is able to be most vehement and relaxed.
prose: From Apollonius: to be free and unwaveringly steadfast, and to look to nothing else, not even for a moment, except to reason; and to remain always the same, in sharp pains, in the loss of a child, and in long illnesses; and to see clearly from a living example that the same person can be both extremely intense and relaxed.

literal: And the [quality] in explanations: not irritable being. And to see a man clearly deeming [himself] least of his own excellences: the experience and the skill about the transmitting the theorems. And the to learn: how it is necessary to receive the seeming favors from friends, neither being overcome on account of these things, nor insensibly passing [them] by.
prose: Also not to be irritable when giving explanations: and to have seen a man who clearly considered his experience and skill in transmitting his theoretical knowledge to others as the least of his own excellences: and how one ought to accept apparent favors from friends, neither being overcome by them so as to compromise oneself, nor passing them by unfeelingly.

literal: From Sextus: the kindly [disposition]: and the example of the household being-ruled-by-the-father: and the concept of the according-to-nature living: and the dignified [character] unaffectedly: and the perceptive [faculty] of friends, caringly: and also the tolerant [disposition] toward laymen, and the unobserving [disposition], of those thinking [themselves to have insight]:
prose: From Sextus: kindliness, and the example set by a household governed by a father's rule, and the concept of living according to nature, and dignity cultivated without artifice, and perceptiveness about friends joined with genuine care for their welfare, and tolerance of laymen, even those who think themselves to have insight.

literal: And also the toward-all-men agreeableness: so-that flattery-than-all on-the-one-hand more-pleasant the intercourse of-him to-be, on-the-other-hand most-respected to-those-same-men in-his-presence at-that-very-time to-be: and also the [being] comprehensively and by-method discovery-capable and ordering-capable of-the necessary-for-life principles:
prose: Also his agreeableness toward everyone, such that his company was more pleasant than any flattery, and yet at that very time most respected by those same people in his presence: also his capacity to grasp things comprehensively and methodically, and his resourcefulness in discovering and ordering the principles necessary for life:

literal: And the never to display an expression of anger or of some other passion: but at the same time to be most free-from-passion, and at the same time most full-of-tender-affection: and the well-spoken quality unostentatiously, and the widely-learned quality without display.
prose: Never to betray any sign of anger or of any other passion, but to be at once utterly free from passion and yet full of tender affection; to be well-spoken without ostentation, and widely learned without display.

literal: From Alexander the grammarian: the not-being-faultfound and the not reproachfully to lay hold of those having brought forward something barbarous or solecistic or ill-sounding, but skillfully to bring forward that very thing only which it was needful to have been said, in the manner of an answer or a joint-testifying or a joint-consideration concerning the very matter itself, not concerning the word, or through some other such tactful side-reminder.
prose: From Alexander the grammarian: to avoid faultfinding, and not to rebuke abusively those who had uttered some barbarism, solecism, or ill-sounding phrase, but skillfully to bring forward, in the manner of an answer, a corroborating testimony, or a joint consideration of the very matter itself, not of the word, only that particular expression which ought to have been used, or through some other such tactful indirect reminder.

literal: From Fronto: the to-take-note-of what-sort-of the tyrannical envy and duplicity and hypocrisy [is], and that, as for-the-most-part, the ones so-called among us well-born-men are somehow rather-lacking-in-affection.
prose: From Fronto: to take note of the sort of envy, duplicity, and hypocrisy that characterize a tyrant, and that, as a general rule, those among us who are called well-born are somehow rather lacking in natural affection.

literal: From Alexander the Platonist: the not often nor without necessity to say to someone or in a letter to write that busy I-am, and not through this manner continually to excuse-oneself-from the according-to-the toward those living-with relations fitting-duties, putting-forward-as-excuse the surrounding affairs.
prose: From Alexander the Platonist: not to say often or without necessity to someone, or to write in a letter, that I am too busy, and not to use this way of continually excusing myself from the duties owed by my relations toward those I live with, by pleading the pressing business that surrounds me.

literal: From Catulus: the not carelessly to hold [it] when a friend complains of something, even if he should happen complaining unreasonably, but to try to restore [him] to the accustomed [footing]: and the [speaking] favorably concerning [my] teachers, ardently: such as [were] the things being recorded concerning Domitius and Athenodotus: and the [disposition] concerning the children truly loving [to be].
prose: From Catulus: not to regard a friend's complaint lightly, even if he happens to complain unreasonably, but to try to restore him to his usual footing; also to speak favorably and warmly about my teachers, as in the anecdotes recorded about Domitius and Athenodotus; and a truly loving disposition toward her children.

literal: From the brother of-me Severus: the love-of-family and love-of-truth and love-of-justice: and also, through him himself: to come to know Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dio, Brutus, and to take a conception of a constitution equality-based, according to equality and equal-freedom-of-speech administered, and of a kingship valuing, of all most, the freedom of those being ruled.
prose: From my brother Severus: love of family, love of truth, and love of justice; and through him I learned to come to know Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dio, and Brutus, and to form a conception of a constitution based on equality, administered according to equality and equal freedom of speech, and of a kingship valuing above all else the freedom of the governed.

literal: And still further from the same [woman]: the evenness and steadfastness in the honor [she showed]: and the beneficence, and the generosity, and the good hope, and the trustfulness concerning being loved by [my] friends: earnestly: and the being-undisguised toward those happening [to be] under condemnation by him: and the not to need conjecture the friends of him about the what he wants or what not he wants, but plain to be:
prose: She also taught me the evenness and steadfastness she maintained in honoring others: to be ready to do good, to give generously, to hope for the best, and to trust confidently and earnestly that I was loved by my friends: and I learned to be open and undisguised toward those who happened to fall under his censure: and I also learned not to need to guess at what my friends wanted or did not want, but to make it plain to them myself.

literal: From Maximus: the mastering of oneself: and according to nothing to be swayed-about: and the good-humor: in both the other circumstances and in illnesses: and also the even-temperedness of character, and gentle and dignified [it was]: and the not complainingly effective [quality] of the things lying-before [him]:
prose: From Maximus: to master oneself and in nothing to be swayed this way and that; to remain good-humored both in other circumstances and in illness; the even temper of his character, and gentleness combined with dignity; and to work through the tasks before him without complaint.

literal: And: the all to believe him, about the things he might say, that so he thinks, and about the things he might do, that not badly he does: and the free-from-wonder and free-from-consternation: and nowhere hurrying, or hesitating, or being-at-a-loss, or downcast, or having-grinned-forcedly, or again being-angered, or being-suspicious:
prose: Also, that everyone should believe of him, concerning whatever he might say, that he really thinks so, and concerning whatever he might do, that he does not act with bad intent: and to be free from wonder and free from consternation, and never in a hurry, or hesitant, or at a loss, or downcast, or forcedly grinning, or again prone to anger, or suspicious:

literal: And the beneficent, and the forgiving, and the truthless: and [I learned]: to provide an impression of [character] unbent rather than being corrected: and that not even would anyone ever have thought to be despised by him: nor would he have endured to suppose someone better than himself [to be]: and also the to-be-graciously-witty:
prose: Also his beneficence, his readiness to forgive, and his freedom from falsehood; and to give the impression of a character naturally unbent rather than merely corrected; and that no one would ever have thought himself despised by him, nor would he have endured to suppose anyone better than himself; and also to be graciously witty.

literal: From the father['s reputation]: the gentle and the steadfast, unshakably abiding by things judged after careful examination. And the being-free-from-vanity regarding the seeming honors: And the industrious and persistent: And also the readiness-to-listen of-those-having something of-public-benefit to-bring-forward: And the unswervingly according-to-merit apportioning to each: And the being-skilled where indeed [there is] need of tension, and where [there is need] of relaxation:
prose: From my father's memory I learned gentleness, and to remain unshaken and steadfast in decisions that have been carefully examined, and freedom from vanity regarding the things that seem to be honors, and to be industrious and persistent, and a readiness to listen to anyone who had some contribution of public benefit to bring forward, and to distribute to each according to merit without ever swerving from it, and the skill of knowing where there is need for tension and where for relaxation.

literal: And the to-stop: the things concerning the loves of the [boys]: and the community-of-mind, and the having-been-granted to friends, not indeed to dine-together with him always, nor to travel-abroad-together, [to be] compulsory, but always the same [him] to be regarded by those left-behind on account of some need: and the being-searching exactly in the counsels, and persistent, but not the to-stand-off-before of the investigation, having been satisfied with the ready-at-hand impressions: and the maintaining [of loyalty] of friends, and nowhere fickle nor frantic [to become]: and the self-sufficient in everything, and the cheerful:
prose: And to put a stop to passions for boys; community of mind; granting one's friends leave not to be obliged always to dine with him or invariably to travel abroad together, but that those who were left behind for some pressing need should always find him unchanged toward them; exact and persistent inquiry in deliberations, never abandoning an investigation prematurely or being satisfied with the impressions that first present themselves; steadfast loyalty toward friends, never becoming fickle or fanatically attached; and self-sufficiency in everything, and cheerfulness.

literal: And: the from-far-off foreseeing, and of-the-least-things the-forearranging, without-tragic-display: and: the suppressed [suppression] of-the acclamations and of-all flattery directed upon him[self], and: the ever watchful-of-necessities [disposition] for the rule, and steward-like of-the provision, and enduring of-the blame-incurring over such things: and: not indeed superstitious concerning gods, nor indeed [to be] popularity-seeking or fawning or crowd-pleasing concerning people, but sobriety in all things, and steadfast and nowhere lacking-in-taste, nor yet innovation-loving:
prose: I learned to plan far ahead and to make provision even for the smallest matters, without theatrical fuss; and to suppress popular acclaim and all flattery directed at oneself, and to be ever watchful over the necessities of rule, and to be a careful steward of expenditure, spending unstintingly on such things, and to endure the blame incurred for such carefulness; and not to be superstitious about the gods, nor, in dealings with people, to court popularity, curry favor, or please the crowd, but to be sober-minded in all things, steady, nowhere lacking in taste, nor given to novelty for its own sake.

literal: And this too: the [thing] which brings something toward easiness of life, of which fortune supplied abundance: to be apt-to-use [it], at once without vanity and without hesitation, so-that, while [such things] are present, to touch [them] unaffectedly, and, while [they] are absent, not to be in need [of them]: And also the [thing], not, however, would anyone say: not indeed that a sophist, not indeed that a home-bred slave, not indeed that a pedant, but that a man ripe, complete, unflattered, being able to manage both his own affairs and [those] of others: [I learned].
prose: She also taught me to use, without vanity yet without hesitation, whatever conduces to the ease of life and whatever abundance fortune supplies of such things, so that when they are present I handle them unaffectedly, and when absent I feel no need of them, spending unstintingly on such things. And also that no one could ever call him a sophist, a home-bred slave, or a pedant, but rather a mature man, a complete one, immune to flattery, and capable of managing both his own affairs and those of others.

literal: In addition to these things, moreover, also the esteeming [disposition] of those truly philosophizing, but toward the others: not reproachful, nor indeed easily-led-astray by them: still moreover the sociable and gracious, not excessively: and [I learned] the caring-for of [one's] own body, in due measure, neither as if someone were fond-of-life, nor for the sake of adornment, nor yet carelessly, but so as: through [one's] own attentiveness, to have need of very few things of medicine, or of drugs and of poultices, from outside.
prose: Besides this, she had genuine esteem for those who truly practice philosophy, while toward the others she was neither reproachful nor easily led astray by them. She also taught me to be sociable and gracious, without excess, and to care for one's own body in due measure, neither as one fond of life nor for the sake of adornment, nor yet carelessly, but so that through such personal attentiveness one had very little need of medicine, or of drugs and poultices from outside.

literal: Especially however: the yielding-without-envy to-those having-acquired some ability, such-as the expressive [ability] or that from-study of-laws or of-customs or of-other certain matters, and the being-eager-along-with them, in-order-that each according to their own merits might-be-well-esteemed: all things according to the ancestral doing, but not this same thing practicing to appear, that is, the ancestral things to guard.
prose: Above all, the readiness to yield without envy to those who possess some particular ability, such as skill in expression, or knowledge derived from the study of laws, customs, or other matters, and to join eagerly with them in their pursuits, so that each might win esteem according to his own merits; and to do everything in accordance with ancestral custom, yet without making a show of cultivating that very custom, but simply guarding ancestral ways.

literal: Still further: the not to-be easily-moved and given-to-flitting, but even in-places and in-affairs the same to-be given-to-abiding: and the [being] fresh immediately and vigorous after the attacks of-the headache with-a-view-to the accustomed works: and the not to-be to-him many the secret-things, but very-few and very-rarest, and these only concerning the common [affairs]: and the sound-minded and measured [quality], both in of-theories completion and of-works arrangements and distributions and in such things: which is of-a-man having-looked-directly toward the very thing needing to-be-done, not toward the reputation upon the things-having-been-done.
prose: She also taught me not to be easily shaken or given to flitting about, but to be steadfast, dwelling on the same places and the same activities, and that right after her headache attacks subsided, she would be fresh and vigorous again at once, ready for her accustomed tasks. I also learned that he did not have many secrets, but very few and very rare, and these only concerning public affairs, and soundness of mind and a sense of measure both in the completion of theoretical studies and in the arrangement and distribution of practical affairs, and in such things generally: the mark of a man who has looked directly at the very thing that needs to be done, not toward the reputation that comes from what has been done.

literal: Not untimely a bather, not fond-of-building, not concerning the foods a deviser, not concerning garments' weaves and colors: not concerning bodies' beauty: the from-Lorium robe leading-up from the lower villa: tunic at Lanuvium, the many [times]: how he made use, toward the one begging-off the cloak at Tusculum, and every such manner [likewise makes use]:
prose: Not to bathe at unseasonable hours; not to be fond of building; not to be inventive about food, or about the weave and color of clothing, or about the beauty of slaves' bodies. I learned about the robe from Lorium that leads up from the lower villa; to wear a simple tunic at Lanuvium for the most part; and how he treated the man who begged off returning his cloak at Tusculum, and every such manner of behavior likewise.

literal: Nothing harsh: nor indeed implacable: nor violent: so-that one-might ever say [of her] anything-of-the-sort. Until sweat: But all-things having-been-allotted: to-be-reckoned, as at leisure, undisturbedly, in-orderly-fashion, vigorously, and harmoniously with themselves.
prose: Nothing harsh, nothing implacable, nothing violent: so that no one could ever say anything of the sort about her; and to persist to the point of sweat; but she taught me that all things are to be reckoned as having their allotted places, as though at leisure, without disturbance, in good order, vigorously, and in harmony with one another.

literal: The [it] to be strong and to endure, and to be sober, in each of the two alike, is of a man having a soul sound and unconquered, such as in the illness, the [illness] of Maximus.
prose: To be strong and to endure, and to be sober in either fortune alike, belongs to a man possessing a soul at once sound and unconquered, such as his was in the illness of Maximus.

literal: From the gods: [I learned] good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good household-members, kinsmen, friends—almost all [of them] good, to have.
prose: From the gods I have had good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good household members, kinsmen, and friends—almost all of them good.

literal: And: the not further to-be-brought-up with the mistress of-the grandfather, and: the youth to-preserve, and: the not before due-time to-be-made-a-man, but still even further to-take-hold of-the time.
prose: And not to be brought up too long with my grandfather's mistress, to preserve my youthful purity, and not to be made a man before the proper time, but even to delay it a while longer.

literal: To be subjected to a ruler and to a father: who was about to take away all the vanity of me, and to lead [me] into the realization of this, that it is possible, while living in a court, neither to need bodyguards, nor conspicuous garments, nor such lamps and statues of a certain kind, and the like ostentation, but it is permitted to contract oneself very nearly to a private citizen, and not on account of this to hold oneself more lowly or more remiss with a view to the things which must be done, on behalf of the common interests, in a leader-befitting manner.
prose: To be subjected to a ruler and a father who was bound to strip away all my vanity and bring me to realize that it is possible, while living at court, not to need bodyguards, or conspicuous robes, or lamps and statues of that sort, or similar ostentation, but that one may reduce oneself very nearly to the condition of a private citizen, without on that account becoming meaner or more remiss with regard to the duties that must be performed on behalf of the common good in a manner befitting a ruler.

literal: To chance upon such a brother: one being able, on the one hand, through character to rouse me toward care of myself; and at the same time also with honor and with affection delighting me: that the children to me not to become without natural gifts, nor as to the little body [ones] distorted: the not-further-me-to-have-advanced in rhetoric and in poetic and in the other pursuits: in which perhaps I might have been held fast, if I perceived myself proceeding well.
prose: To have such a brother, one able through his character to rouse me to care for myself, and at the same time to delight me with the honor and affection he showed me: to keep my children from being born without natural gifts, and from being deformed in body: not to make further progress in rhetoric, poetry, and the other pursuits, in which I might perhaps have become absorbed, if I had perceived myself advancing easily in them.

literal: The to-outrun the tutors and in honor to-establish [them], of-which indeed they-seemed to-me to-desire, and not to-postpone [it] in-hope of-my, since [they] were-still young, later this-same-thing to-do: the to-know: Apollonius, Rusticus, and Maximus.
prose: Not to outrun my tutors but to establish them in honor, which they indeed seemed to me to desire, and not to postpone this in the hope, since they were still young, that I would do it later: and through them to come to know Apollonius, Rusticus, and Maximus.

literal: The to-be-imagined concerning the according-to-nature of-life, clearly and often: such as someone is, so that, as-much-as depends on the gods and on the from-there dispensations and cooperations and inspirations, nothing to-hinder me from-now living according to nature; and to-fall-short still of-this through my own fault and through the not diligently-keeping the from-the-gods remindings and almost teachings:
prose: To form a vivid and frequent picture of what a life lived according to nature is like, so that, as far as depends on the gods and on the communications, dispensations, and inspirations that come from them, nothing should any longer prevent me from living in accordance with nature; and to fall short of this still, through my own fault and through not heeding the reminders—almost the very instructions—coming from the gods.

literal: The to-hold-out for-me the body to-such-an-extent, in such a life: the neither to-have-touched of-Benedicta nor of-Theodotus, but also later, in erotic passions having come to be, to be sound: the having-become-angry oftentimes at Rusticus, to do nothing more, in respect of that in which I might afterward have changed my mind: the: about-to (die young, having-borne her) nevertheless to dwell with me the last years.
prose: That my body held out for so long enduring such a life; that I never touched Benedicta or Theodotus, but even later, when caught up in erotic passions, recovered my soundness of mind; that though I often grew angry with Rusticus, I never went so far as to do anything I would afterward regret; that though she was destined to die young, she nevertheless chose to spend her last years living with me.

literal: The [fact] that, as often as I was wished to help someone being-poor or unto some other thing needing, never to hear me: that there is not to me money, whence it might come to be: and: the same to-me need similar, as from another to receive-a-share, not to fall-together: the [fact] that the wife to be such: so on the one hand submissive, and so affectionate, and so unpretentious: the: to be well-supplied [with] proper tutors unto the children:
prose: As often as I wished to help someone in need or in want of something else, I never had to hear that there was no money for it, and I never fell into a like need myself, so as to have to receive from another. She taught me that a wife could be so submissive, so affectionate, and so unpretentious. I learned to be well supplied with proper tutors for my children, spending unstintingly on such things.

literal: The through dreams: that helps were given, both other things and, so as not to spit blood and not to feel dizzy; and of this also, in Caieta, [an oracle telling] just as you will treat [yourself]: The [fact] how I desired philosophy, not to fall into some sophist, and not to sit down to the composing [of treatises], or to analyzing syllogisms, or to being occupied about the meteorological [matters]: For all these things: they require gods helping and fortune. The [things written]: among the Quadi, at the Granua.
prose: That through dreams remedies were given, among others, both against spitting blood and against dizziness, and also, at Caieta, an oracle telling how you would be treated, just as you were treated. That when I conceived a desire for philosophy, I did not fall into the hands of some sophist, nor waste my time writing treatises, working out syllogisms, or occupying myself with speculations about the heavens. For all these things require the gods' help and fortune's favor as well. Written among the Quadi, on the river Granua.
